claims.text: In the jobs most exposed to AI, workers in their early twenties fall behind workers over fifty [cite:canaries], while in the least exposed jobs they do not.

claims.text: Agents take hold first in job search, property and other matching markets.

claims.text: The labs earn a growing share of their revenue from products and deployments inside their customers' firms rather than from selling access to their models by the token.

claims.text: Much of AI's everyday work moves out of distant data centres onto people's own phones and laptops.

claims.text: Firms increasingly buy AI's work through a party with assets and a licence that can be held liable, such as an established service firm.

claims.text: Law, contracting and other trades scattered by place stay split among many small firms, while the AI tools each trade uses gather around a few vendors.

claims.text: A frontier lab launches or majority-owns a professional services firm, under its own brand or at arm's length, by September 2028.

claims.text: Firms in AI-exposed industries do not all grow bigger by 2029; they consolidate in infrastructure and splinter in applications.

claims.text: Groups that run many unrelated businesses with AI come to be valued above the sum of their parts.

claims.text: Firms in the industries most exposed to AI do not shrink towards nothing as agents cut the cost of dealing.

claims.text: Firms keep inside the work that would reveal what they know, and independent agents dealing for firms in open markets stay rare.

The reading is developers' routed tokens, not firms' spending, and the rival speaks of who runs a model, not whose it is, so it accepts the same reading. A router's traffic is all rented, so this reading can show spread among sellers and cannot show renting against owning.

The census is a screen scored by AI models, not a record of observations, so no nightly test reads it.

claims.text: A group that runs many businesses with AI is valued above the sum of its parts only if it shares what each learns across them; a holding company that keeps them apart is not.

claims.text: Through 2028, firms that adopt AI shrink their entry-level and junior ranks before they remove layers of management.

claims.falsifier: A later count finding the layers of adopting firms unchanged or rising, or the flattening explained by something other than AI. This site holds no count of layers.
claims.text: Within a few years of adopting AI, firms have fewer layers between the people who do the work and the chief executive than similar firms that have not adopted it.

claims.text: Through 2030, firms that no person runs or answers for stay rare in lawful, regulated trades, because someone has to decide in the cases no instruction covers and answer for the result.

essay:
# A firm rents what it can check and owns what it must answer for.

A firm is a line drawn round some work. Inside it, people are told what to do; outside it, things are bought. Economists have long explained where the line falls by what it costs to deal with strangers. AI models are now sold by the token, a fragment of a word, so a firm can buy thinking by the unit as it buys electricity. This essay asks where the line moves when that is so, and sets out what this site's records show. The title is this site's own reading, argued in the third folio; no one writer cited here makes it whole.

### Folio I · the boundary

## A firm ends where buying gets cheaper than managing

Ronald Coase, a British economist, asked in 1937 why firms exist if prices can settle who makes what. His answer was that using a market is not free. Someone has to find out prices, bargain, and write a contract for every exchange: the transaction costs. Inside a firm a manager's instruction replaces all of that. A firm, "that little planned society" as he later called it, grows until organising one more job inside costs as much as buying it outside [cite:coase].

An AI agent, a model set to carry out tasks on someone's behalf, can search, compare and bargain for almost nothing. Peyman Shahidi, John Horton and their colleagues, who study online markets, called the prospect a Coasean singularity, the point at which dealing costs almost nothing, with a question mark, and expect the line between making and buying to move [cite:shahidi_etal]. One of them works for Amazon and another is a paid adviser to Anthropic. They do not say firms vanish, and they list new frictions agents bring.

Coase's rule has two sides, and cheap intelligence lowers both. Gillian Hadfield, who designs legal and regulatory systems for AI, and Andrew Koh, who studies how to design markets, observe that what stops a firm growing without limit is a set of obstacles that "seem intrinsic to humans but not to AI" [cite:hadfield_koh]. So the rule cannot say by itself whether firms shrink or grow. Something else decides, and the next three folios take the candidates in turn: what a firm knows, what it must answer for, and where its decisions have to be taken.

### Folio II · the leak

## Asking the market for help tells it what you know

Soren Larson, who writes about how money moves between AI labs, the companies that train the largest models, and the apps built on them, turns Coase round. If every firm rents the same models, what separates one firm from another, once trust and customers' attention are set aside, is context: what it knows about its customers, its costs and its plans. To buy from a market a firm has to say what it wants, and saying so reveals context. Even a request for bids tells rivals what the firm thinks matters. On his account the firm exists "to prevent the extraction of its scarce context" [cite:larson_coasean]. The cost of dealing has not fallen. It has changed from the cost of finding a seller into the cost of being seen.

Two older results explain why no market repairs this. Kenneth Arrow, an economist who studied how markets handle knowledge, showed that a buyer cannot tell what information is worth until he has it, and then need not pay [cite:arrow]. George Akerlof, who studied markets in which sellers know more than buyers, showed that when quality cannot be seen, good goods are withdrawn and the market shrinks [cite:akerlof]. A firm cannot sell its context without giving it away, or buy another's without guessing at its quality. So it keeps what it knows and acts on it itself.

The two sides predict different things. Shahidi and his colleagues expect agents to search and bargain across markets for whoever deploys them; Larson expects them to stay inside the firm or be kept off other firms' platforms. This site holds no record that tests it. A count of firms buying knowledge-heavy work through independent agents would settle it, and nobody publishes one.

### Folio III · the liability

## Whoever must answer for the work ends up owning it

Sanford Grossman and Oliver Hart, economists who studied contracts, asked in 1986 what ownership is for. No contract can list everything that might happen. Where it is silent someone has to decide, and they defined owning an asset as holding that right: "Ownership is the purchase of these residual rights" [cite:grossman_hart]. Ownership has a price, since control given to one party is taken from another, so it should rest with the party whose decisions matter most.

Hadfield and Koh point out that instructing an AI is a contract of this kind: what a designer tells a model to aim at can never cover every case [cite:hadfield_koh]. They ask who answers when it goes wrong, and find the law unready, since few legal systems hold anyone liable for acts they could neither foresee nor control.

This site joins the two, and the join is its own reading, not theirs. If an agent's instructions are incomplete, someone must decide in the gaps and bear the loss, and Grossman and Hart's result says that someone should own the operation. Byrne Hobart, who writes The Diff, a newsletter on finance and technology, arrives there from the buyer's side. Once software acts for long stretches with some randomness, the buyer asks whom to sue. A small seller of agents has the least to lose, so the work is bought from a firm with assets, customers and a name to lose, and a seller sure of its software may do best to own the business that uses it [cite:hobart_sued]. He notes in passing that insurance written for agents is beginning to be sold. Christian Catalini, Xiang Hui and Jane Wu, economists who study the cost of verifying work, add that doing gets cheaper with computing power while checking is held up by people's time, so the profit moves to whoever can verify the work and stand behind it [cite:catalini].

The rival view is that insurance and contract will carry the liability, so nobody need own anything. Over the past year this site has recorded [fact:insurer_ledger] moves by insurers to write AI's mistakes out of their standard policies. One of those moves was an insurer selling separate cover for AI as it took it out of the standard policy. Both sides expect exclusions first. They part on what comes next: cover for AI sold widely, which would favour the rival, or operators absorbing the risk. Nobody publishes the premiums written for such cover, so tonight's reading cannot tell them apart.

### Folio IV · the edge

## Knowledge can be sent to the centre; acting on it sometimes cannot

Friedrich Hayek, an economist who studied how prices carry what people know, argued in 1945 that much of the knowledge an economy runs on is "the knowledge of the particular circumstances of time and place" [cite:hayek], which no central office can collect, so decisions belong with the person on the spot.

Erik Brynjolfsson, who directs Stanford's Digital Economy Lab, and Zoë Hitzig, who studies AI's effects on society, argue that AI undoes much of this. Hitzig worked at OpenAI when they wrote and has since joined a research institute run by Anthropic. It records what used to go unwritten and lets a head office process far more, so they predict "larger average firm size, greater industry concentration, and reduced local managerial autonomy" [cite:brynjolfsson_hitzig]. This site sets beside them a finding they do not cite. Rich Sutton, a computer scientist who studies how machines learn, found that over decades of AI research, methods built on what experts know were beaten by general methods that improve as computing gets cheaper [cite:sutton]. He was writing about research, not firms; the reading across is this site's.

Chris Walker, who writes on the economics of unwritten knowledge, replies that writing knowledge down for a model is neither free nor complete. Choosing what a model needs to know for each task takes local judgement and has to be done again as the work changes. "The knowledge problem has not been solved", he writes; it has moved upstream [cite:walker_context]. Larson grants that context can be gathered and still ends at the edge, the place where the work is done: running a model costs energy and time, and a car at speed cannot wait for an answer from a distant data centre [cite:larson_hayek].

The camps agree on more than their conclusions suggest. Both draw a line between what can be recorded and what cannot, and both leave time-critical decisions at the edge: Brynjolfsson and Hitzig themselves list decisions that must be taken faster than a message can travel, beside rare cases, bodily skill and whatever the law reserves for people. They differ on whether the line moves. Brynjolfsson and Hitzig think the exceptions may shrink as models improve; Walker expects each new ability to open new work that needs local judgement. Delay is the floor neither side disputes, and energy is Larson's addition. Brynjolfsson and Hitzig name the test, whether firms that adopt AI move decisions to the centre; Walker's own dated predictions turn on firm size, and no one holds a series that reads either.

### Folio V · the rent

## Most firms should rent intelligence; a few should own it

There are two reasons to rent. The lead is short: open models, whose trained settings are published for anyone to run, trail the best closed ones by [fact:open_lag], so a firm that trains its own is buying something that loses value fast. And most firms see nothing in their own work that others do not see: in a simulation of his own, Larson found that a system trained on other firms' results did better than one trained on a firm's own history [cite:larson_router]. Luis Garicano, an economist who studies how firms organise what they know, and Jesús Saa-Requejo put it plainly: "Intelligence is not what stops most organisations from doing what they want to do" [cite:garicano_theses].

The risk in renting is set out by Garicano and Saa-Requejo too. A supplier of rented intelligence can raise its price once a firm's work depends on it, and can learn the firm's business by watching how it is used [cite:garicano_holdup]. That is Larson's leak again, with the lab as the party watching. Their remedy is not to own the model. It is to rent it, to own the rules and records that sit above it, and to keep a second supplier within reach. So the answer turns on what is scarce in the firm's own work.

[plate:regimes]

Clayton Christensen, who studied why leading firms lose their lead, gave the general rule: when one part of a product becomes good enough and interchangeable, the profit moves to the neighbouring part that still limits performance [cite:christensen]. Intelligence by the token is becoming that part. Larson cautions against his own case: owning every step does not make a firm safe, because AI also makes it cheap to stitch separate pieces into something good enough [cite:larson_vertical].

### Folio VI · the residue

## Some things do not get cheaper when intelligence does

Philippe Aghion, Benjamin Jones and Charles Jones, economists who study growth, argued that when tasks depend on one another, growth may be held back by "what is essential and yet hard to improve" [cite:aghion_jones_jones]. Value collects at whatever stays slow, and inside a firm several things do.

Attention: a customer has the same hours in the day whatever a model costs. Ben Thompson, who writes on technology strategy at Stratechery, showed how firms that own the relationship with users make their suppliers interchangeable [cite:thompson]. Accountability: a model cannot be sued, fined or struck off, and a firm can. Trust: one of the answers Akerlof named for quality nobody can see was a name with something to lose. Permission: licences, regulators and courts decide who may act, and Brynjolfsson and Hitzig count them among the limits on their own prediction. And unwritten judgement: knowing what good work looks like in a trade.

The last is the one most likely to give way. If models come to learn on the job, what is unwritten today is recorded tomorrow, and Walker says he is wrong if general agents manage complex work inside firms without continuing human help by 2028.

### Folio VII · the shape

## The pyramid thins where work can be checked, and keeps whoever must answer

A firm is drawn as a pyramid for a reason. Garicano argued in 2000, with a model, that a hierarchy is a way to economise on knowledge. The many at the base handle the common problems and pass the exceptions up to people who know more: "a knowledge-based hierarchy is a natural way to organize the acquisition of knowledge" [cite:garicano_hierarchies]. Nicholas Bloom, Garicano, Raffaella Sadun and John Van Reenen, who measure how firms are managed, later found that cheaper technology pulls two ways. Cheaper information gives people lower down more to decide; cheaper communication sends decisions back to the centre [cite:bloom_it_ct]. They studied plants before AI, their paper does not say which of the two AI is, and this site has found no study that settles it.

Luke Drago and Rudolf Laine, who write on AI and the economy and now work at Thinking Machines, which builds AI, argue that AI empties the pyramid from the bottom. Firms first stop hiring at entry level, the jobs people start in, then lose their juniors, then their managers, until at a few there is nobody left [cite:drago_laine_pyramid]. They give no dates and call the last step their most speculative. They mean large white-collar firms, and say policy or technology could change the course. Dario Amodei, who runs Anthropic, the company whose model drafted this page, has warned of the same first step: that "AI could displace half of all entry-level white collar jobs" within a few years [cite:amodei_adolescence]. He says could, not will.

The evidence offered for that first step is a study of payroll records by Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar and Ruyu Chen: workers in their early twenties have fallen behind in the jobs most exposed to AI, mostly because fewer are hired, not because more leave or are let go [cite:canaries]. Zanna Iscenko and Fabien Curto Millet, economists at Google, which sells AI, objected to an earlier version that hiring in those jobs turned down before ChatGPT was released, as interest rates rose; they do not say entry-level work is safe later [cite:iscenko_curto_millet]. The revised study says the gap remains after allowing for interest rates, and its authors call it an early sign, not proof of a cause.

Others expect the middle to go. Jack Dorsey, who runs the payments company Block, and Roelof Botha, a partner at the venture firm Sequoia, write of Block's own plans that a model of the whole company can carry what managers used to pass along: "There is no need for a permanent middle management layer" [cite:dorsey_botha]. They report no results and say parts of the plan will likely break. The one measurement this site has found is by Michael Ewens and Xavier Giroud, economists who estimated from online résumés how many layers of reporting listed American firms have. They report that "they flatten their hierarchies following the adoption of artificial intelligence" [cite:ewens_giroud]; their summary does not say which layers go, or that AI is the cause.

Garicano himself expects more managers, in a post written to say Amodei is wrong. A job is a bundle of tasks that is often costly to pull apart, and a firm is a coalition of people who want different things. Someone has to decide between them where no contract or rule does, be blamed for the result, and be seen as fair. AI could in principle come to hold that standing, he grants, but the law has built nothing to give it; until it does, "some human will have to hold the residual decision rights" [cite:garicano_task], the right to decide whatever was not settled in advance. Julia Shin and Sandra Sucher, who write on management, found in a small set of interviews at two consulting firms that checking AI's work fell on the managers in the middle [cite:shin_sucher_middle]. At the far end, Shawn Bayern, a law professor, argued that American company law already allows an entity that follows a program and that no person owns or controls [cite:bayern_entities]. Lynn LoPucki, another, accepts that and expects crime to use it first [cite:lopucki_entities].

[plate:shapes]

Writers of fiction drew several of these shapes first, and the lane below the table lists a few. They are fiction, and nothing here rests on them.

This site keeps a census of American office work. AI models judged, task by task, whether the work could be handed to software, which here means that a check existing today can settle quickly and cheaply whether it was done right. It is a screen scored by models, not a forecast, and it cannot see rank. It has no field for seniority, so it reads occupational groups, kinds of job, not junior against senior within one. So it cannot test Drago and Laine's order. What it shows is this. The share of payroll that passes the screen is largest for office support and sales, and smallest for legal work; managers are near the bottom on the headline vote, though not when every model must agree. In no group does most of the payroll pass, and in every group more of it is held back only for want of a check than passes.

[plate:jobs]

On the shape, what follows is this site's judgement. Rank is the wrong axis. The work that goes is the work an existing check can settle, wherever it sits, and on the census more of that lies in the lower-paid kinds of job than among managers. What stays is setting the task, checking where no check exists, and answering for the result. So the pyramid thins most at the base. Whether the middle narrows is not settled: the one count of layers says firms flatten, and the census finds little of a manager's work passing. And the firm keeps a top for as long as the law wants a person to answer. The cost is one Garicano names: the base was also where people learned the trade, and a firm that trains fewer juniors makes fewer seniors [cite:garicano_becker].

### Folio VIII · the limit

## In the limit, a firm is a name that can be sued, holding what cannot be bought

What follows is this site's judgement. It joins arguments that each have a test into a picture that has none.

Carry each argument to its end and the firm stops being a body of people who do the work. It specifies: it decides what is worth doing and what counts as done. It holds scarce things: customers' attention and trust, licences, sensors, sites with power. It bears risk: it is the legal person that pays when the work is wrong. And it rents its thinking by the token from whoever sells it cheapest, apart from small models it runs on the spot where delay or secrecy demands.

[plate:anatomy]

On the size of such firms the theories part, and this site keeps all three. Brynjolfsson and Hitzig expect larger firms and more concentrated industries, and Hadfield and Koh see a pull the same way. Dwarkesh Patel, a podcaster who interviews AI researchers, writing with two co-authors and putting his own confidence low, expects much larger firms and thinks a single one is not inevitable, because "The market continues to serve as the grounding outer loop" [cite:patel]. Walker and Larson each expect a barbell. Walker's has very large firms where the work is generic and many small ones close to each trade; Larson's has very large firms that keep what they know to themselves and many small ones. Larson also expects groups that own many businesses and share what each learns to be worth more than their parts [cite:larson_conglomerate]. Firm size by industry, and the value of such groups against their parts, would separate these, and this site cannot yet read either.

Who profits, on this reasoning, is not mainly the seller of tokens. In Larson's own model a lab captures about a quarter of what its tokens are worth to the buyers, and less as open models catch up [cite:larson_complexity]. The rest goes to the owners of what is scarce beside the intelligence, and, where firms compete, to their customers.

### Folio IX · the record

## Buyers are acting on this before anyone can show it pays

Several of this site's records bear on the argument. Roll-ups, buyers that gather many small firms into one and plan to run them with AI, bought [fact:rollup_service_deals] firms that sell services, such as accounting practices and letting agents, in the past year that this site could find, against [fact:rollup_service_deals_year_ago] the year before. The count comes from one search of the larger roll-ups this site follows, so it is a floor; older announcements are the likeliest to have been missed, which flatters the rise; and some buyers announce firms as joining them without stating a stake. What they buy, on this site's reading, is customers and licences. Their purchases of software products, [fact:rollup_software_deals] in the same year, are counted apart.

The labs are moving the same way. They and the companies that sell computing made [fact:lab_deals_now] purchases in the layers above them, hirings of whole teams included, in the latest year this site has searched. Among them is a firm that fits AI into other companies' work, which OpenAI agreed to buy as it launched a company that it says it majority-owns and controls. Anthropic formed a services venture with outside investors in the same month; the reports this site holds do not say who owns how much, so it is not in this reading. That count's rule leaves out ordinary businesses, so it would miss a lab buying an accounting practice.

Suppliers are binding customers without buying them. Commitments signed in which a seller of chips or computing also funds the lab that buys from it, by a stake, a guarantee, a backstop or a contract to pay whether or not the capacity is used, came to [fact:seller_funded] over the past four quarters. That is the face value promised, not money paid, and a few very large deals make up most of it. On this site's reading it is a way to bind a customer short of owning it; only the stakes carry any right to decide.

The check matters more than the task. This site's census screens American knowledge work for whether it could be handed to software. On its count, the payroll that passes the screen is far smaller than the payroll held back for one reason only: no existing check settles whether the work was done right. The figures are on the census page, since a screen scored by models is not a reading this essay can test.

None of this shows that owning pays. [fact:firms_using_ai] of American firms say they used AI in the past fortnight, a pace this site calls normal. The site holds no margin for any roll-up after a purchase. The census could not measure whether an owner keeps a saving, and it was scored by three AI models, one of them made by Anthropic, whose model also drafted this page. The site's figures on firm size run years late, and nothing here records where decisions are taken. The site's own leans, a model's judgement on claims too early to test, run against two threads of this essay: they doubt that AI's work will increasingly be bought through firms that can be sued, and that groups of pooled businesses will be valued above their parts. A count of purchases records what buyers believe. Each claim below says what would prove it wrong.

positions.case: None of the writers this page read argues that firms vanish, and [fact:firms_using_ai] of American firms say they use AI at all, so any change in the size of firms lies ahead of the readings.
positions.kill_shot: Firms in the industries most exposed to AI shrinking sharply as work moves to independent contractors and their agents.
positions.mechanism: Agents cut the cost of finding, bargaining and contracting, and they cut the cost of managing as well, so both sides of Coase's comparison fall [cite:coase]. The authors who named the Coasean singularity put a question mark on it themselves and list the new frictions agents bring [cite:shahidi_etal].
positions.title: Cheap agents move the firm's boundary; they do not remove it

positions.case: This site holds no reading that favours it.
positions.kill_shot: Firms in exposed industries keeping or growing their size as agents spread.
positions.mechanism: If a firm exists only because dealing with outsiders is costly, then agents that deal for almost nothing leave little reason to employ anyone. This is the popular reading of the Coasean singularity; no writer this page read holds it as stated.
positions.title: With dealing nearly free, most work is bought in and firms shrink towards nothing

positions.case: Larson points to the largest retail platforms shutting out independent shopping agents in favour of their own.
positions.kill_shot: Independent agents dealing on firms' behalf at scale in open markets.
positions.mechanism: When everyone has the same models, what a firm knows about its own needs is its edge, and asking the market for help gives it away.
positions.title: Asking reveals what you want, so firms keep work inside

positions.case: Selling a house is easier to delegate than buying one, and the first traction is in job search, property and matching.
positions.kill_shot: Agents spreading first in markets where people rarely hire human agents.
positions.mechanism: Handing a task to an agent is easiest where people already hire agents and can say simply what they want.
positions.title: Agents arrive first where wants are simple and agents already work

positions.case: Buyers built around AI bought [fact:rollup_service_deals] firms that sell services in the past year, against [fact:rollup_service_deals_year_ago] the year before, and insurers have moved [fact:insurer_ledger] times in a year to write AI's mistakes out of their standard policies. Neither reading shows that owning pays.
positions.kill_shot: Sellers that own no operation and hold no licence carrying the liability for consequential AI work by contract and insurance, at scale.
positions.mechanism: An instruction to an agent cannot cover every case [cite:hadfield_koh], so someone must decide in the cases it missed and pay when the work is wrong. Where a contract cannot be completed, ownership settles who decides [cite:grossman_hart]; so the party that bears the loss wants to own the operation, and a seller with nothing to lose is a poor party to buy from [cite:hobart_sued]. None of these writers makes the whole argument; this site joins them.
positions.title: Whoever must answer for the work ends up owning the operation

positions.case: The forecasts board on this site, a model's judgement, leans this way; it expects insurers to sell cover written for AI and doubts that AI's work will mostly be bought through firms that can be sued.
positions.kill_shot: Insurers going on writing AI out of standard cover while cover written for it stays small.
positions.mechanism: If insurers learn to price an agent's mistakes, a software seller can buy cover and warrant its work, as contractors do, and the buyer need not care who owns what.
positions.title: Insurance and contract carry the liability, so nobody needs to own the operation

positions.case: Hobart expects labs to buy operating firms in the trades they serve, gaining customers and assets that can answer for mistakes.
positions.kill_shot: Buyers taking AI's work on long, unpredictable tasks from parties that cannot answer for its mistakes.
positions.mechanism: When an agent does long, unpredictable work, the buyer wants someone with assets and a licence who answers for its mistakes, so AI reaches customers through such parties.
positions.title: AI's work is bought through firms that can be sued

positions.case: Early evidence, by the authors' account, fits bigger firms and less local autonomy.
positions.kill_shot: Firms getting smaller and more decentralised as they adopt AI.
positions.mechanism: AI captures the local knowledge that used to justify leaving decisions to people on the spot.
positions.title: Decisions move to the centre

positions.case: Walker sets his prediction explicitly against the view that AI makes every firm bigger.
positions.kill_shot: Firms growing larger across AI-exposed industries, applications included.
positions.mechanism: Codifying a firm's knowledge for AI is costly, lossy and needs upkeep, so scale pays where the work is generic, in computing and models, while firms closest to a trade's own knowledge win in applications.
positions.title: Big at the base, small at the top

positions.case: The knowledge Hayek meant is local and fleeting and cannot be gathered into statistics; this site adds that a model trained on what is written may lack it.
positions.kill_shot: Firms that move decisions to the centre with AI outperforming those that leave them local.
positions.mechanism: What matters for most decisions is knowledge of particular times and places, which changes constantly and by its nature cannot reach the centre as statistics. Hayek argued it about central planning; this site carries it to AI.
positions.title: Knowledge on the spot keeps decisions there

positions.case: Open models a few steps behind the best keep getting better, and each release widens what a device can do on its own.
positions.kill_shot: Everyday use staying in cloud data centres even as capable open models shrink.
positions.mechanism: Once a small model on a phone or laptop is good enough, running it there is cheaper and faster than paying a data centre for each request, and the meter stops.
positions.title: AI's everyday work moves onto people's own devices

positions.case: Open models trail the best closed ones by [fact:open_lag], and developers' routed tokens are spread across many labs.
positions.kill_shot: Firms that train and run their own models pulling ahead of rivals that rent, in trades where no firm senses anything the others cannot.
positions.mechanism: The best model's lead over open ones is short, so a firm that owns its intelligence owns a wasting asset; and most firms see nothing in their own work that others do not see, so a system that learns from many firms beats one that learns from one [cite:larson_router]. What holds most organisations back is workflow, authority and data, not intelligence [cite:garicano_theses].
positions.title: Most firms should rent intelligence and own something else

positions.case: The labs have been buying firms in the layers above them, their own customers' trades among them.
positions.kill_shot: Firms moving freely between suppliers of models at no loss, and no supplier entering its customers' trades.
positions.mechanism: A supplier of rented intelligence sees how its customer works, can raise its price once the customer's work depends on it, and can learn enough to compete [cite:garicano_holdup]. Garicano and Saa-Requejo answer by renting the model while owning the rules and records above it and keeping a second supplier. This site carries their warning further, to the case for owning the model itself.
positions.title: A firm that rents its thinking teaches its supplier its business

positions.case: Code that comes with tests is handed to AI before contracts that come with none.
positions.kill_shot: Work that is hard to check being handed over as fast as work that is easy to check.
positions.mechanism: A task is handed over when checking the result costs less than doing it. Hadfield and Koh argue about accountability; this site carries the argument to the order of adoption.
positions.title: What goes first is set by the cost of checking, not the cost of doing

positions.case: In the jobs most exposed to AI, young workers have fallen behind older ones; in the least exposed jobs they have not.
positions.kill_shot: Young workers falling behind in the least exposed jobs as well, which would point to a cause other than AI.
positions.mechanism: A firm that can do a junior's work with AI hires fewer juniors before it lets anyone go.
positions.title: Junior hiring shows it first

positions.case: Workers in their early twenties have fallen behind in the jobs most exposed to AI, mostly through less hiring; the authors call it an early sign, not proof of a cause [cite:canaries]. Economists at Google objected that hiring in those jobs turned down before ChatGPT was released [cite:iscenko_curto_millet]; the revised study says the gap remains after allowing for interest rates.
positions.kill_shot: Firms that adopt AI removing layers of management while they go on hiring at entry level.
positions.mechanism: Entry-level work is the simplest and the cheapest to hand to a model, so a large firm first stops hiring at the bottom, then loses its juniors, then its managers as later systems do longer and harder work, and last its executives [cite:drago_laine_pyramid]. Its authors give no dates, call this the default course for large white-collar firms and not a certainty, and call the last stage their most speculative.
positions.title: AI empties the pyramid from the bottom

positions.case: A count of layers at listed American firms finds them flattening after they adopt AI [cite:ewens_giroud]; its abstract does not say which layers go or that AI is the cause.
positions.kill_shot: Firms that adopt AI keeping their layers of management while their entry-level ranks shrink.
positions.mechanism: Much of a manager's work is passing information up and instructions down. When a model can carry both, a firm needs fewer layers between the people who do the work and the people who answer for it [cite:dorsey_botha].
positions.title: The middle goes, and the firm flattens

positions.case: On this site's census, legal work has the least payroll passing its hand-over screen and office support the most; managers are near the bottom on the headline vote, though not when all three scorers must agree. The census is a screen scored by AI models and has no field for seniority.
positions.kill_shot: Firms running consequential work in lawful trades with no person who decides or answers for it.
positions.mechanism: A firm is a coalition of people who want different things, and where no contract or rule settles a matter someone has to hold the right to decide and bear the result, a standing the law does not yet give AI [cite:garicano_task]. Checking a model's work falls to the people in the middle [cite:shin_sucher_middle]. This site carries both further: the layers that stay are the ones that answer, sign or check, whatever their rank.
positions.title: A firm keeps people where someone has to answer

positions.case: This site holds no count of firms that no person runs. A law professor who accepts that they can be formed expects them to be used first for crime [cite:lopucki_entities].
positions.kill_shot: Firms that no person runs staying rare and marginal while models go on improving.
positions.mechanism: Company law already allows an entity that follows a program and that no person owns or controls [cite:bayern_entities], and the authors of the pyramid essay expect a small number of firms to end with no human employees, the step they call their most speculative [cite:drago_laine_pyramid]. The head of one lab expects a company of a single person to be valued very highly [cite:altman_one_person]. None says such firms will be common; this site states the strong form so it can be tested.
positions.title: A firm needs no person to run it

positions.case: Hoffman points to founders folding their companies into AI-run groups and to industrial chiefs who say the old case for scale has run out.
positions.kill_shot: AI-run groups trading below the sum of their parts, as conglomerates did.
positions.mechanism: AI lets one centre see and run many unrelated businesses, removing the overhead that made conglomerates trade at a discount.
positions.title: The conglomerate comes back

positions.case: Cloud computing escaped the same trap by becoming software, and the leading chip foundry by being almost alone.
positions.kill_shot: The labs' revenue staying mostly in selling access to their models by the token.
positions.mechanism: Selling access to a model tends towards a commodity business, so labs move into products and into deployments built into their customers' work, where switching is costly.
positions.title: Labs escape by moving up the stack, and lock their customers in

columns: What is scarce in the firm's work
regimes.note: This site's reading of the writers cited on this page. It is a judgement, and no row has a test of its own; the last row rests on no source and is the weakest.
regimes.places_note: Most firms sit in the first row. The rows are the cases in which this site judges owning wins; they are fewer firms than the first row holds.
rows: Nothing the firm alone can see, and a cheap check exists
Answering routine customer queries; keeping the books
Rent by the token, from more than one seller
The firm's customers, once rivals rent the same; and whoever pools many firms' results
A signal only this firm senses
A fleet of driverless cars; a ring that reads its wearer's body (both among Soren Larson's examples)
Own the sensors and the model trained on what they read
The owner-operator, for as long as the signal stays its own
Time or power at the point of work
A vehicle at speed; a camera running on a battery
Own small models and run them on the spot
Whoever owns the device or the site
The right to sign, and the loss when the work is wrong
An audit opinion; a prescription; an insurance policy
Rent the model, own the licensed operation
The licensed firm, and whoever insures it
Secrecy, where being seen is the loss
A trading strategy; a product not yet announced
Keep the model inside, on machines the firm controls
The firm, and sellers of private installations
The frontier itself
Training the most capable model
Own
The labs, for as long as their lead lasts
Use so heavy and steady that paying by the token costs more than running machines
A service that calls a model at every step for every user
Run an open model on owned or leased chips
The firm, and the owners of chips and power
regimes.title: When to rent intelligence, and when to own it

shapes.note: Each row is its authors' hypothesis in this site's words. None is tested here, and several come from people who sell AI or advise on it; the sources say who.

rows.shape: A pyramid emptied from the bottom
rows.stays: The executives longest; at a few firms nobody
rows.who: Luke Drago and Rudolf Laine; Dario Amodei warns of its first step
rows.would_show: Young workers' hiring falling in the jobs most exposed to AI while managers' numbers hold

rows.goes_first: Managers whose work is passing information along
rows.shape: A flatter firm, with the middle taken out
rows.stays: People who do the work, and people answerable for a result
rows.who: Jack Dorsey and Roelof Botha argue it; Michael Ewens and Xavier Giroud measure flatter firms and do not say which layer goes
rows.would_show: Fewer layers at firms that adopt AI than at similar firms that do not

rows.goes_first: The routine work by which juniors paid for their training
rows.stays: Seniors, each overseeing more; later, too few of them
rows.would_show: Firms hiring fewer trainees and paying more for experienced staff

rows.goes_first: Jobs made of a single task
rows.stays: Whoever holds the right to decide, and whoever checks the machine's work
rows.who: Luis Garicano; Julia Shin and Sandra Sucher report the middle loaded with checking, not enlarged
rows.would_show: The share of managers and reviewers rising at firms that adopt AI

rows.goes_first: On Altman's remark, most hired staff
rows.shape: A very small firm directing many agents
rows.stays: A founder or a few people who set the task and judge the result
rows.who: Sam Altman, in a remark Fortune reported; Ethan Mollick reports agents organising themselves and says it could mean more work for people
rows.would_show: Large companies with a handful of employees becoming common

rows.goes_first: By assumption every human worker; what they add is that copies need no hand-offs
rows.shape: A firm of copies of its best worker
rows.stays: Many copies of a few models, and the market as the test of their work
rows.who: Dwarkesh Patel and his co-authors, who put their own confidence low
rows.would_show: Firms growing very large without adding layers

rows.goes_first: The human owners and whoever controlled the firm; it may still hire people
rows.shape: A firm that no person owns or controls
rows.stays: A legal entity that follows a program
rows.who: Shawn Bayern; Lynn LoPucki, who accepts it can be done and warns against it
rows.would_show: Such entities trading lawfully at scale

shapes.title: Shapes the firm might take, and who argues each

sources.field: a British economist who asked why firms exist when prices can co-ordinate work
sources.finding: A firm exists because using a market has costs: finding out prices, bargaining and writing a contract for each exchange. A firm grows until organising one more job inside costs as much as buying it outside or having another firm do it.
sources.venue: Economica, 1937. The link opens his Nobel lecture of 1991, The Institutional Structure of Production, which restates the argument and is where the quoted words come from; the 1937 article was read in a scan of the journal's pages
sources.work: The Nature of the Firm

sources.field: economists and a computer scientist who study online markets; Fradkin works for Amazon and Horton is a paid adviser to Anthropic
sources.finding: Agents could slash the cost of searching, bargaining and contracting; they will be taken up first where people already hire human agents and can state simply what they want, and platforms will set rules for how outside agents may use them, much as websites tell search engines' crawlers what they may read, though some already block them.
sources.venue: The Economics of Transformative AI (National Bureau of Economic Research)
sources.who: Peyman Shahidi, Gili Rusak, Benjamin Manning, Andrey Fradkin and John Horton
sources.work: The Coasean Singularity? Demand, Supply, and Market Design with AI Agents

sources.field: Hadfield designs legal and regulatory systems for AI; Koh studies how to design markets and incentives
sources.finding: AI agents lack the identity and registration systems markets rely on; the authors sketch two routes, each with its own problems, one tying each agent to a registered person or firm that answers for it, the other giving agents legal standing with assets a court could seize.
sources.quote: seem intrinsic to humans but not to AI
sources.venue: The Economics of Transformative AI (National Bureau of Economic Research)
sources.work: An Economy of AI Agents

sources.field: a writer on how money moves between AI labs and the apps built on them, who co-founded Crosshatch, a personalised-AI start-up whose closure he announced in November 2025
sources.finding: Cheap agents make dealing with outsiders costlier, not cheaper, because asking a market for anything reveals what you want to your competitors; so firms keep work inside, platforms shut out outside agents, and firms split into the very large and the very small.
sources.quote: to prevent the extraction of its scarce context
sources.work: Against The Coasean Singularity

sources.field: an economist who studied how markets handle knowledge and risk
sources.finding: Information is a good that markets handle badly: a buyer cannot tell what it is worth until he has it, and once he has it he need not pay; and using it tends to reveal it. One private remedy is a large company that runs many projects and insures itself.
sources.venue: The Rate and Direction of Inventive Activity (National Bureau of Economic Research and Princeton University Press), 1962. The link opens the chapter's record; it was read in the Bureau's own copy
sources.work: Economic Welfare and the Allocation of Resources for Invention

sources.field: an economist who studied markets in which sellers know more than buyers
sources.finding: Where sellers know the quality of what they sell and buyers do not, everything sells at a price for the average, owners of good goods withdraw, and the market can shrink to nothing. Guarantees, brand names and licences grew up as answers.
sources.venue: Quarterly Journal of Economics, 1970. The link opens the journal's record; the article was read in a scan of the journal's pages
sources.work: The Market for "Lemons": Quality Uncertainty and the Market Mechanism

sources.field: economists who studied contracts and what ownership is for
sources.finding: No contract can list every decision about an asset, so ownership is the right to decide whatever the contract leaves out. Giving that right to one party takes it from another and blunts the second party's reason to invest, so one firm should own another only when the gain outweighs that loss.
sources.quote: Ownership is the purchase of these residual rights
sources.venue: Journal of Political Economy, 1986. The link opens the journal's record with the abstract; the article was read in full in a scan of the journal's pages
sources.work: The Costs and Benefits of Ownership: A Theory of Vertical and Lateral Integration

sources.field: the writer of The Diff, a newsletter on finance and technology, after work in digital advertising and investment research
sources.finding: As agents take on long, unpredictable work, buyers pay for a party with assets that can be held liable, so established service firms stand between AI and the customer.
sources.work: Paying Up for the Right to be Sued

sources.field: economists who study what it costs to verify work
sources.finding: The cost of having a machine do a task falls with computing power, while the cost of checking the result is held up by people's time. So people's capacity to verify becomes the limit on growth, and the profit moves to whoever holds trustworthy ground truth and underwrites the liability.
sources.venue: arXiv preprint; not yet published in a journal
sources.who: Christian Catalini, Xiang Hui and Jane Wu
sources.work: Some Simple Economics of AGI

sources.field: an economist who studied how prices carry what people know
sources.finding: The knowledge an economy runs on is scattered among the people on the spot and never exists whole in any one place, so decisions about particular circumstances have to be left to them, with prices telling them what they need to know.
sources.quote: the knowledge of the particular circumstances of time and place
sources.work: The Use of Knowledge in Society

sources.field: Brynjolfsson directs Stanford's Digital Economy Lab; Hitzig studies AI's effects on society, now at the Anthropic Institute and at OpenAI when the chapter was written
sources.finding: AI can capture the local, unwritten knowledge that once argued for leaving decisions to people on the spot, so decisions centralise, with bigger firms, more concentrated industries and less room for local managers.
sources.quote: larger average firm size, greater industry concentration, and reduced local managerial autonomy
sources.venue: The Economics of Transformative AI (National Bureau of Economic Research)
sources.work: AI's Use of Knowledge in Society

sources.field: a computer scientist who studies how machines learn
sources.finding: Across decades of AI research, methods that build in what people know helped for a while and then stalled, and were overtaken by general methods, search and learning, that improve as computing gets cheaper.
sources.work: The Bitter Lesson

sources.field: writer on the economics of tacit knowledge and AI at the Out of Sample newsletter
sources.finding: Chris Walker argues that feeding AI the right context stays costly, lossy and local, so by 2029 firms in AI-exposed industries grow larger at the infrastructure layer but split into smaller specialists at the application layer.
sources.quote: The knowledge problem has not been solved
sources.work: Context Engineering: Why Hayek's Knowledge Problem Survives AI

sources.field: a writer on how money moves between AI labs and the apps built on them, who co-founded Crosshatch, a personalised-AI start-up whose closure he announced in November 2025
sources.finding: Context can now be gathered and put in front of a model, which weakens Hayek's original point; what cannot be centralised cheaply is the running of a model, which costs energy and time, so intelligence is placed where the work is.
sources.work: The Bitter Lesson and Hayek's Revenge

sources.field: a writer on how money moves between AI labs and the apps built on them, who co-founded Crosshatch, a personalised-AI start-up whose closure he announced in November 2025
sources.finding: A neutral router that pools many firms' checked outcomes learns to solve their problems, new kinds above all, faster than any one firm alone, so paying for AI by the outcome belongs with it; in his simulation the model was held fixed, and what won was a harness trained on other firms' outcomes.
sources.work: Router Power

sources.field: Garicano is an economist who studies how firms organise what they know; Saa-Requejo is his co-author at the Silicon Continent newsletter
sources.finding: The sellers of models are squeezed between customers who can switch with a change of setting and suppliers above them who cannot be replaced. The surplus goes to hardware and to whoever does the work of fitting AI into an organisation, where the limits are workflow, authority and data.
sources.quote: Intelligence is not what stops most organisations from doing what they want to do
sources.work: Three theses on AI value capture

sources.field: Garicano is an economist who studies how firms organise what they know; Saa-Requejo is his co-author at the Silicon Continent newsletter
sources.finding: A firm that rents its models can be squeezed by its supplier: on access, on price, by work that will not move to another model, and by the supplier learning the firm's own know-how from the way it is used. Their remedy is to rent the model, own the layer above it and keep a second supplier.
sources.work: How to avoid being held up by the labs

sources.field: Christensen studied why leading firms lose their lead; Raynor and Verlinden are his co-authors on this article
sources.finding: While a product is not yet good enough, the money goes to whoever builds the integrated system that fixes what is lacking. Once it is more than good enough the design becomes modular, the assembler becomes interchangeable, and the profit moves to the parts that now limit performance.
sources.venue: Harvard Business Review, 2001. The article is paywalled after its opening; the argument was read in a transcript of a talk Christensen gave in 2004
sources.who: Clayton Christensen, Michael Raynor and Matthew Verlinden
sources.work: Skate to Where the Money Will Be

sources.field: a writer on how money moves between AI labs and the apps built on them, who co-founded Crosshatch, a personalised-AI start-up whose closure he announced in November 2025
sources.finding: Owning every step of the work is the best strategy but is not safe by itself, because AI makes it cheap to stitch separate pieces into something good enough. He lists the conditions under which an owner of the whole chain holds, and concedes that they move.
sources.work: An Equilibrium Theory of Vertical Integration

sources.field: economists who study where growth comes from
sources.finding: Tasks depend on one another, so output is limited by the tasks that are hardest to improve. As automated tasks get cheap their share of spending falls, and the slow, essential tasks that are left take a rising share.
sources.quote: what is essential and yet hard to improve
sources.venue: National Bureau of Economic Research working paper, 2017. The link opens the paper's record with the abstract; the working paper was read in full
sources.who: Philippe Aghion, Benjamin Jones and Charles Jones
sources.work: Artificial Intelligence and Economic Growth

sources.field: a writer on technology strategy at Stratechery
sources.finding: A firm that owns the relationship with users at scale makes its suppliers interchangeable: they join on its terms. Such a firm serves each new user at no extra cost and does not operate the supply it gathers.
sources.work: Defining Aggregators

sources.field: an economist who studies how firms organise what they know
sources.finding: A firm's hierarchy economises on knowledge: those at the base learn the common problems and pass the exceptions up to fewer people who know more. It says nothing about AI.
sources.quote: a knowledge-based hierarchy is a natural way to organize the acquisition of knowledge
sources.venue: Journal of Political Economy; the abstract was read, on its RePEc record
sources.work: Hierarchies and the Organization of Knowledge in Production

sources.field: economists who measure how firms are managed and organised
sources.finding: In plants studied before AI, cheaper information went with more autonomy lower down and more people reporting to each manager, while cheaper communication went with less autonomy and more decisions at the centre. It does not say which of the two AI is.
sources.venue: National Bureau of Economic Research working paper, later in Management Science; the abstract was read
sources.who: Nicholas Bloom, Luis Garicano, Raffaella Sadun and John Van Reenen
sources.work: The Distinct Effects of Information Technology and Communication Technology on Firm Organization

sources.field: writers on AI and the economy who ran Workshop Labs and, on their own account, now work at Thinking Machines, which builds AI
sources.finding: AI empties the white-collar pyramid from the bottom: entry-level hiring stops first, then junior roles go, then managers, then nearly everyone but the executives, then the executives, and at a small number of firms every employee. They give no dates, call this the default course for large white-collar firms and not a certainty, and call the last stage their most speculative.
sources.venue: The Intelligence Curse; the page carries no date, and an earlier version appeared in February 2025
sources.work: Pyramid Replacement

sources.field: chief executive of Anthropic, which sells AI and whose model drafted this page
sources.finding: He repeats a warning he gave in 2025, that AI could displace a large share of entry-level office jobs within a few years even as it speeds growth. He says could, not will.
sources.quote: AI could displace half of all entry-level white collar jobs
sources.work: The Adolescence of Technology

sources.field: economists at Stanford's Digital Economy Lab who study AI and work through payroll records
sources.finding: Employment of workers in their early twenties in the jobs most exposed to AI has fallen behind that of their less exposed peers, mostly through less hiring, while experienced workers show no such gap. The authors describe the pattern; they do not claim to have proved its cause.
sources.who: Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar and Ruyu Chen
sources.work: Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence

sources.field: economists at Google, which sells AI
sources.finding: Job postings in the occupations most exposed to AI peaked before chatbots were released, in step with rising interest rates, and a general hiring freeze shrinks a narrow age band by arithmetic; so the fall in young workers' employment is not yet evidence of AI. They do not say AI will leave entry-level work alone later.
sources.who: Zanna Iscenko and Fabien Curto Millet
sources.work: Looking for the Ladder: Is AI Impacting Entry-Level Jobs?

sources.field: Dorsey runs Block, a payments company; Botha is a partner at Sequoia Capital, a venture firm
sources.finding: Hierarchy exists to pass information along, and a model of the whole company can carry it instead, leaving people who do the work, people answerable for a result for a fixed term, and playing coaches. They report no results and say parts of it will likely break.
sources.quote: There is no need for a permanent middle management layer
sources.work: From Hierarchy to Intelligence

sources.field: economists who estimated from online résumés how many layers of reporting listed American firms have
sources.finding: Listed American firms are pyramids of several layers; they add layers after listing and flatten after adopting AI. The abstract does not say which layers go or that AI is the cause.
sources.quote: they flatten their hierarchies following the adoption of artificial intelligence
sources.venue: National Bureau of Economic Research working paper; the abstract was read
sources.work: Corporate Hierarchy

sources.field: an economist who studies how firms organise what they know
sources.finding: A job is a bundle of tasks and a firm a coalition with conflicts, so someone must hold authority and bear the consequences; he expects more managers, whose work is handling what is ambiguous, and grants that the junior ladder is disrupted. He allows that AI could in principle hold such authority once the law provides for it.
sources.quote: some human will have to hold the residual decision rights
sources.work: The task is not the job

sources.field: Sucher is a professor of management practice at Harvard Business School; Shin is a graduate of the school who worked at a consultancy owned by PwC
sources.finding: In interviews at two consulting firms, juniors and partners gained from AI while middle managers took on checking its output and coaching their teams to use it. It shows the middle loaded, not grown.
sources.venue: Harvard Business Review; the part of the article open on the page was read
sources.work: AI Adoption Is Overloading Your Middle Managers

sources.field: a law professor who studies the law of business entities
sources.finding: He argues that American company law already lets a limited company bind itself to follow a program and its human members then withdraw, leaving a legal entity that no person owns or controls, which may still employ people. It is an argument about what the law permits, which other scholars dispute, not a report that such firms exist.
sources.quote: they are already possible under current law
sources.venue: European Journal of Risk Regulation; the abstract and the notes printed on the page were read
sources.work: The Implications of Modern Business-Entity Law for the Regulation of Autonomous Systems

sources.field: a law professor who studies bankruptcy and company law
sources.finding: Entities with no human controllers can be formed under most company laws, would be used first for crime and other harm, and are hard to regulate because jurisdictions compete to charter them.
sources.venue: Washington University Law Review; the abstract was read
sources.work: Algorithmic Entities

sources.field: an economist who studies how firms organise what they know
sources.finding: A professional firm's pyramid both spreads its seniors' knowledge and trains its juniors, who pay for the training with routine work. AI lets a senior oversee more while doing that routine work, so firms train too few successors.
sources.work: The AI Becker problem

sources.field: Patel hosts a podcast of interviews with AI researchers; Erdil and Besiroglu are his co-authors on this essay
sources.finding: A firm of AI workers can copy its best worker and merge what the copies learn, so dealing inside the firm gets cheaper and firms grow much larger. One giant firm is not inevitable, because planning inside still needs profit and loss outside to say whether it is working. The authors put their own confidence low.
sources.quote: The market continues to serve as the grounding outer loop

sources.field: a writer on how money moves between AI labs and the apps built on them, who co-founded Crosshatch, a personalised-AI start-up whose closure he announced in November 2025
sources.finding: Groups that own many businesses have been valued below their parts because managers spread thin lose to focused ones. He argues the discount turns into a premium for groups that share what each business learns and keep it from leaking, and not for a holding company that keeps its businesses apart.
sources.work: The Conglomerate Premium

sources.finding: In a model of his own, a lab's price touches only the task at the margin and everything above it goes to the user, so the lab captures a minority of what its tokens are worth to buyers, and less as open models catch up.

sources.field: Narayanan is a Princeton computer scientist; Kapur, a senior fellow at New America, studies how AI is governed
sources.finding: Selling access to frontier models tends towards a commodity business, where competition likely pushes prices to cost, so the labs' likeliest path to lasting profit is moving up the stack into products and deployments built into their customers' work, which escapes the trap at the price of lock-in. The builders of past infrastructure rarely kept the value, with cloud computing and the leading chip foundry as partial exceptions.
sources.work: Up the Stack: How AI's Escape From the Commodity Trap Risks Enterprise Lock-in

sources.field: an investor at Pace Capital who writes about where computing happens
sources.finding: For much everyday work the cheapest and fastest place to run AI will be the device that already holds the data, so demand for inference in distant data centres will turn over slowly, then suddenly.
sources.venue: an essay he shared as a public document

sources.finding: Trades that are scattered by place, such as law and contracting, stay split among many firms, while the AI tools each one uses gather around a few vendors.

sources.field: the writer of The Diff, a newsletter on finance and technology, after work in digital advertising and investment research
sources.finding: AI spreads through industries wrapped inside existing structures such as firms and licences, and ads in chat assistants can work because assistants see what people want to buy earlier than search does.
